reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Congenital cataract may occur in isolation or as part of a wider syndrome, so a systemic evaluation is essential
Presents with leukocoria, an absent or abnormal red reflex, nystagmus, or failure to fixate in infancy
Metabolic causes such as galactosaemia are important because they are treatable and may be reversible if caught early
Associated syndromes include chromosomal disorders such as trisomy 21, and conditions such as Lowe syndrome, myotonic dystrophy and congenital infection (part of a wider differential)
Bilateral cataracts more often have a metabolic, genetic or systemic cause, whereas unilateral cataracts are more often sporadic and local
Dense central cataracts cause deprivation amblyopia, so timely surgery within the critical period of visual development is crucial
A careful family history and examination of parents can reveal an inherited pattern, often autosomal dominant
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital cataract is an opacification of the lens present at or soon after birth, arising when the normal transparency and orderly arrangement of lens fibres is disturbed during development. In syndromic forms this may result from mutations in genes encoding lens crystallins, membrane and cytoskeletal proteins, or developmental transcription factors, or from systemic metabolic derangements (such as abnormal galactose metabolism) that alter the osmotic and biochemical environment of the lens. Chromosomal abnormalities and multisystem genetic syndromes disrupt lens development as one of several affected tissues. A dense opacity blocks formation of a clear retinal image during the sensitive period, causing amblyopia unless treated promptly.
additionalDifferentials: Retinoblastoma and other causes of leukocoria
Corneal opacity from anterior segment dysgenesis
additionalInvestigations: Red reflex testing and slit-lamp or handheld examination to characterise the opacity
Metabolic screen including tests for galactosaemia and relevant urine and blood studies
Systemic and dysmorphology assessment for associated syndromic features
Ocular ultrasound where the fundus cannot be visualised, to assess the posterior segment
Chromosomal and molecular genetic testing guided by the clinical picture
redFlags: Dense bilateral cataract in an infant requiring urgent referral to prevent amblyopia
Associated systemic illness or failure to thrive suggesting a metabolic disorder
Signs of raised intraocular pressure or coexisting glaucoma
Leukocoria where retinoblastoma has not yet been excluded
reference.prognosis: Visual outcome depends on the density and laterality of the cataract and the timeliness of surgery and amblyopia therapy; early treatment of bilateral cataracts and of reversible metabolic causes can give good vision, whereas late-treated dense unilateral cataracts often have a guarded prognosis.
pitfalls: Missing a treatable metabolic cause such as galactosaemia by omitting a metabolic screen
Delaying surgery beyond the critical period and allowing irreversible deprivation amblyopia
Treating the cataract as isolated and failing to look for syndromic or systemic disease
Overlooking coexisting glaucoma or posterior segment pathology
references: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Perform early cataract surgery (lensectomy) within the critical period for dense or visually significant opacities to prevent deprivation amblyopia
Treat reversible metabolic causes promptly, with dietary galactose restriction for galactosaemia
Provide postoperative optical correction with aphakic contact lenses, spectacles or intraocular lens, and continue amblyopia therapy
Undertake systemic and metabolic evaluation and manage the underlying syndrome
Monitor for postoperative complications, particularly glaucoma and visual axis opacification
Offer genetic counselling and family assessment for heritable forms
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across paediatric ophthalmology, clinical genetics and paediatrics
